conditions.raw: 1500 K selected for accelerating the simulations

statement: In the reactive molecular dynamics study, crystalline silica was dissolved in sodium hydroxide solution after establishing the elevated-temperature acceleration scheme.

evidence.supports: Explicitly states that sodium hydroxide solution was employed to dissolve crystalline and amorphous silica after selecting 1500 K for acceleration.
The final sentence identifies reactive MD simulations as the authors' own-study method.

To achieve better temporal sampling, we implemented an
elevated temperature strategy in the canonical ensemble
(NVT) to accelerate the simulation. However, before
proceeding with this approach, it was crucial to confirm
that the reaction pathways at elevated temperatures were
comparable to those at room temperature. To address this,
we utilized well-tempered metadynamics (WTMetaD)
to compare the reaction pathways of silica dissolution
at different temperatures (300, 700, 1000, and 1500 K).
Through the free-energy reconstruction provided by
WTMetaD, we determined that 1500 K was suitable for
accelerating the simulations while maintaining a dis-
solution process consistent with that observed at room
temperature.
Once the acceleration scheme was established, we
employed a sodium hydroxide solution as an electrolyte to
dissolve both crystalline and amorphous silica. Structural
parameters, such as bond lengths/angles and coordina-
tion distributions of silicon and sodium, were statistically
analyzed to investigate the phase assemblage of the MD
models at elevated temperatures (700, 1000, and 1500 K).
Moreover, we delved into the details of surface disso-
lution kinetics to quantify the stepwise transformation
rates from fully linked SiO networks (Q4) to aqueous

The findings of this study reveal that the silica sur-
face follows a stepwise dissolution mechanism, involv-
ing the continuous breaking of Si–O–Si bonds on the
solid surface. In alkaline electrolyte solutions, silicon
atoms on the surface often adopt a temporary pentacoor-
−
dinate structure with OH ions, facilitating the rupture
of Si–O–Si bonds. However, due to the high energy bar-
rier associated with silica dissolution, conventional direct
dissolution simulations are typically limited by their rare
event sampling nature. Enhanced methods, such as meta-
dynamics, have been employed to improve the sampling
efficiency of rare dissolution events in silica. Furthermore,
the kinetic Monte Carlo method has been proposed to
study the long-term dissolution process of silica, enabling
kinetic sampling across multiple timescales.19

ing the dissolution kinetics of silica at the atomic scale,

surface reactions, as well as the differences in dissolution
